title: Spec sheet, export label and a price that pays
course_title: Export Readiness (Selected Products): From Local Seller to First Export Shipment

say: Spec sheet, export label, and a price that pays.
This is the video for Module 2 of Export Readiness.
Foreign buyers judge you on paper before they taste or touch anything. They want a written specification, and a label that follows their country's law, not only NAFDAC's.

panel.heading: Buyers judge you on paper first
items: A spec sheet says exactly what they get
A label that follows their country's law
A carton that survives the journey
A price built up from your real costs

say: Your carton must survive lifting, stacking and humid sheds. And your price must be built up from real costs. Many first exports lose money because the price was the local price plus something.

panel.heading: Buyers judge you on paper first
items: A spec sheet says exactly what they get
A label that follows their country's law
A carton that survives the journey
A price built up from your real costs

say: A specification, or spec sheet, describes exactly what the buyer will receive. It also helps your helpers make the product the same way every time.
Quality limits, such as maximum moisture, differ between buyers. Do not invent them. Copy the buyer's own numbers into your sheet.
Give every batch a lot number, print it on every bag, and keep a retained sample of each lot. If a complaint comes months later, you can check where the fault started.
For example, Hauwa in Kano packs 1 kg bags of dried hibiscus. Her importer's rule is simple: no bag below 1,000 g. She weighs 10 bags picked from the start, middle and end of packing.

panel.heading: Hauwa checks ten bags from one lot
items: Lowest 996 g and 998 g: two fail
Raise the target to 1,010 g, recheck all

say: The average is 1,007.4 g, which looks fine. But one bag is 996 g and another 998 g. Two of ten break the rule.

panel.heading: Hauwa checks ten bags from one lot
items: Lowest 996 g and 998 g: two fail
Raise the target to 1,010 g, recheck all

say: She raises her filling target to 1,010 g, tops up every light bag, and records the change. The average alone would have hidden the problem.

panel.heading: Hauwa checks ten bags from one lot
items: Lowest 996 g and 998 g: two fail
Raise the target to 1,010 g, recheck all
panel.rule: Check the lowest bag, not only the average.

say: For example, Ada in Enugu sells a 200 g ginger pepper mix. A London shop wants it. Her label has no ingredients, a date nobody can check, and the claim no chemicals, which means nothing, because salt is a chemical.

panel.heading: Ada fixes her label for a UK shop

say: Her new label lists ingredients by weight, prints a real best before date with storage advice, and adds the UK importer's details. She checks the smallest letters are at least 1.2 mm high.

panel.heading: Ada fixes her label for a UK shop

say: Allergens can make people seriously ill. In the UK and EU, 14 allergens must be emphasised, for example in bold. Sesame is one, so Ada puts it in bold.

panel.heading: Three label rules that protect people

cards.d: UK and EU law names 14 allergens, such as sesame and peanuts. Emphasise them in the ingredients.
Shea creams and soaps need a responsible person in the UK or EU before retail sale.
Remove any claim you cannot prove, such as 'cures' or 'no chemicals'.

say: Creams and soaps fall under cosmetics law there. Do not ship them for retail until a partner in that market agrees to act as responsible person.

say: Use new double-wall cartons sized so items cannot move. Line them for dried foods, and tape in an H pattern.
Before your first shipment, drop one packed carton from waist height on its bottom, a corner, an edge and a side. Then mark every carton, for example 1 of 6, matching your packing list exactly.

panel.heading: Pack to survive the journey
items: Liner for dried foods, space filled
Tape in an H pattern, top and bottom
Drop test before your first shipment
Shipping marks match the packing list

say: Incoterms are rules from the International Chamber of Commerce. Each one says where your costs and risk end. Under Ex Works, the buyer does everything, which can be hard with Nigerian export formalities.

panel.heading: Where your costs and risk stop

cards.d: Goods ready at your premises. The buyer does everything else, even export clearance.
Handed to the buyer's carrier at a named place, export-cleared. A good first choice.
You pay sea freight and insurance, but risk passes once goods are on board.

say: Free Carrier, F C A, is often the best first choice. Your costs stop at a place you know, such as your forwarder's warehouse.

panel.heading: Where your costs and risk stop

cards.d: Goods ready at your premises. The buyer does everything else, even export clearance.
Handed to the buyer's carrier at a named place, export-cleared. A good first choice.
You pay sea freight and insurance, but risk passes once goods are on board.

say: Under CIF you pay freight to the destination port, but the risk passes at loading. Always write the rule, the named place and Incoterms 2020 on every quote.

say: Amina builds her price up from her own records, per kilogram.

card.title: Amina builds her FCA cost per kg

say: Product and packing cost 2,550 naira per kg. Road transport and documents to her forwarder in Lagos add 600 per kg.

card.title: Amina builds her FCA cost per kg

say: That is 3,150 naira. She adds a 20% margin, making 3,780. At an example rate of N2,000 to the pound, that is £1.89. She adds a 5% currency buffer: £1.98 per kg, FCA Lagos, valid for 14 days.
For CIF Felixstowe, she adds freight and insurance: £2.71 per kg.

card.title: Amina builds her FCA cost per kg

say: To remember. Take quality limits from the buyer. Check the lowest bag, not just the average. Label to the destination's law and emphasise allergens.
Build your price up from cost, name the Incoterm, and add a currency buffer and a validity period.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Take quality limits from the buyer
Build the price up, add a buffer
